title: Closing Out the School Year: A Letter to My Colleagues
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Writing as the 2021-22 school year closes, Dave reflects on a shift in his own motivation, from chasing recognition and originality to simply trying to tell the truth, borrowing a C. S. Lewis line about originality as a byproduct of honesty rather than a goal in itself. He names a few convictions he holds "deep in his bones" about schools as places of human flourishing across every discipline, announces a month-long publishing pause for the summer, and closes with an earnest, personal note of appreciation to fellow teachers.
points: Uses a C.S. Lewis quote — originality comes as a byproduct of trying to tell the truth, not of pursuing originality itself — to reframe his own decade of writing and teaching away from recognition-seeking.

Names a core conviction: schools can be places of "human flourishing" that promote long-term student growth across every discipline, not just English/literacy, when teachers aren't too stressed and distracted to pursue it.
Frames a full month of publishing silence as an intentional practice, not neglect — "there's a time for quiet" — modeling the same boundary-setting he preaches to teachers about their own workload.
Closes with direct, unguarded appreciation for colleagues' labor across the year, positioning the piece as personal correspondence rather than generic year-end messaging.
quotes: Even in literature and art, no man who bothers about originality will ever be original: whereas if you simply try to tell the truth (without caring twopence how often it has been told before) you will, nine times out of ten, become original without ever having noticed it.
I think this sums up this past school year for me, as a teacher in the classroom and a writer on this blog: I've not tried to be original, but I have tried to tell the truth.

Schools can be places of human flourishing, centers of love and learning; they can do this as they promote the long-term flourishing of young people by teaching them toward mastery in the disciplines and the arts.
These things aren't impossible, but they are rare: because we forget, because we get distracted, because we're stressed and under pressure.
Because there's a time for quiet. And though I love the writer's discipline, I love even more being the change I'd like to see in the world.
I tell you what, colleague — it may sound cheesy or disingenuous, but in my heart and my will and my mind there is an earnestness for you, the work you've done, and the work you'll do.
